PLANT GUIDE · AGLAONEMA 'LADY VALENTINE'

Aglaonema 'Lady Valentine'

Aglaonema commutatum 'Lady Valentine' — Chinese evergreen · Araceae, the arum family

Grown for its pink-splashed leaves — and this November it did the rare thing: it bloomed. The green hood rising out of the foliage is a true flower structure, built on the same plan as a peace lily's. This guide covers the plant, its bloom, and the two-phase reproductive dance that bloom performs.

🔍 Anatomy — What It Looks Like

The leaves are the whole show: broad, lance-shaped blades whose centers run rose-pink, splashed and speckled with green, with green margins and midribs. That pink-dominant pattern is what keys this plant to 'Lady Valentine'.

The stems are upright fleshy canes that leaf out as they climb, and the plant clumps from the base — new shoots rise beside the old ones, which is how a single pot fills in.

In the wild the genus grows on shaded rainforest floors across Southeast Asia — which is why it tolerates indoor light that would starve most plants, and why its pink is a cultivated flourish, bred in by growers.

🌸 The Bloom — a Spathe & a Spadix

What looks like one green bud is an inflorescence — a whole cluster of tiny flowers packed onto one structure, the signature design of the arum family.

The spathe is the hood: a single modified leaf, green and fleshy, wrapped around the spike like a cloak. In your photos it is still closed, with just the pale tip of the spike peeking out.

The spadix is the spike inside — a fleshy finger covered in hundreds of minute flowers: female flowers at the base, male flowers above, with a bare stretch between them. No petals, no show — it was built for insects in a dim understory, not for eyes.

🔄 The Blooming Cycle

When — and why. Indoors, a bloom can arrive in any month, but late winter through summer is its season, as the days lengthen and the house warms. It takes a mature plant — usually three to five years old — settled into steady warmth, humidity, and bright indirect light: read it as a plant established enough to reproduce. The honest footnote: a stressed plant can also bloom, as a last-ditch effort to set seed — the company it keeps (strong leaves, steady growth) tells you which story is yours.

  1. The bud rises. A green spear pushes up from a leaf axil near the base of a stem — the closed spathe, holding the folded spadix. This is your first two photos.
  2. The spathe unfurls — usually at night — and the pale spadix stands revealed. Your third photo catches the first moment of this.
  3. Female phase. The flowers at the base of the spadix become receptive first, for about a day.
  4. Male phase. Roughly two days later, the upper flowers ripen and shed pollen — after the females have closed. The bloom cannot pollinate itself.
  5. The fade. Unpollinated, the spathe browns, the spadix softens, and the whole structure withers away over one to three weeks.
  6. If pollinated: berries swell along the lower spadix, ripening green to yellow to red over four to six months — one seed inside each.

🐝 Reproduction — the Two-Phase Dance

That staggered timing has a name — protogyny — and a purpose: females first, males second, so a bloom can only be pollinated by a different bloom. It is the plant's built-in defense against inbreeding.

In the wild, the couriers are small understory insects — tiny beetles and fungus gnats — moving pollen bloom to bloom. The genus holds 21 species, all open-pollinated, and a wild stem makes only three to five flowers a year.

Breeders who create cultivars like this one cheat the calendar with gibberellic acid (GA3) sprays that force many plants to flower at once, then carry pollen by hand and wait months for seed. At home, seed is slow — and a cultivar's seedlings won't come true anyway. 'Lady Valentine' is a clone: multiply it by division and cane cuttings, not seed.

📋 The Care Card

LightBright, indirect. It survives low light, but the pink is paid for in light — dim corners wash the color toward green.
WaterEvenly moist, never soggy. Let the top inch dry, then water through; empty the saucer.
WarmthA true tropical — happiest at 65–85°F, sulky below 60, and kept clear of cold drafts and dry heat vents.
HumidityAverage rooms are fine; grouping plants or a pebble tray keeps leaf edges from crisping in winter.
FeedingLight and regular in spring and summer — a balanced houseplant feed at half strength, monthly.

✂️ Keep the Bloom, or Cut It?

A bloom is expensive: while it lasts, the plant diverts energy from leaves to flowers, and new leaves can come in smaller and duller. That is why many growers snip the bud the moment it appears.

Keeping it harms nothing on a healthy plant — it is the plant's full life cycle, and a houseplant bloom is uncommon enough to be worth watching once. This one is mid-performance right now.

🌿 If you cut: use clean snips, follow the bloom's stalk to its base, and cut close without nicking the stem. The plant redirects everything back to foliage within days.

🩺 Common Problems

Root rotThe real killer — wet feet in a pot without drainage. Mushy stems at the base mean act fast: dry it out, trim rot, repot fresh.
MealybugsWhite cottony specks hiding in the leaf axils. Dab them off with a swab of rubbing alcohol.
Fading pinkAlmost always light: too dim, and the plant trades its pink for more green to photosynthesize. Move it brighter, gradually.
Brown leaf tipsDry winter air or inconsistent watering. Steady the rhythm before reaching for remedies.
⚠️

Calcium oxalate — handle with respect. All parts of Aglaonema, berries included, carry needle-like oxalate crystals: chewing brings burning and swelling of mouth and throat in cats, dogs, and people. Beautiful on the shelf — keep it out of nibbling range.
